findings.title: Launch control switches on at every stop and idle falls to 593 rpm
evidence: Seen 6 times in 3 logs. The numbers below are from the lowest one.
RPM fell to 593 against a 1,100 target and stayed under 80% of target for 3.0 s.
Ignition was 0.0° during the dip. Steady idle in these logs runs 12.0°.
MAP rose to 88 kPa. Steady idle sits at 31 kPa.
Lambda reached 1.23 with short-term fuel trim at −14.7%.
Intake cam was at 0.4° against a 10.0° target.
States that differ from steady idle: Ignition Active Table 3 (normally 2), Launch Control State 1 (normally -5).
Launch Control State changed to 1 on 6 occasions, each as road speed fell below 3 km/h with the accelerator at 0%.
findings.why: At 0° of timing the engine makes far less torque from the same air. The idle controller has to open the throttle to hold speed, manifold vacuum is lost, and the engine can stall as the car stops.
steps: In the launch control setup, add an arming condition a stopped, idling car cannot meet: a minimum accelerator position (80% is a common choice) or a dedicated switch. Road speed alone arms it at every stop.
If it has to arm on speed alone, edit the ignition table it switches to (Ignition Active Table 3): put idle timing, 12°, in the cells below 2,000 rpm instead of 0°.
Re-log a stop from a roll. Ignition should hold near 12° and MAP near 31 kPa as the car comes to rest.

channels.a: O2 Control Bank 1 Short Term Fuel Trim

findings.title: Lean of target under boost
evidence: Lambda held 0.87 against a 0.80 target at 5,224 rpm, 156 kPa.
Short-term trim was +0.8%, long-term −0.5%, injector duty 49%.
This is the highest load in the logs. Nothing above it has been tested.
findings.why: Running leaner than target under boost raises combustion temperature. It is the usual route to knock and piston damage, and it gets worse as boost goes up.
steps: Add 9% to the fuel table around 5,000 rpm / 160 kPa (0.87 ÷ 0.80 with the trims included).
Carry the same 9% into the cells above 160 kPa and past 5,000 rpm before you go there. They are untested, and an untested cell should start rich.
Leave boost and timing where they are until a repeat pull holds lambda on target.

channels.a: O2 Control Bank 1 Short Term Fuel Trim

findings.title: Closed-loop fuel target swings ±0.10 λ at idle
evidence: O2 Control Bank 1 Target is 0.10 λ away from Target Lambda in 3,485 of 3,509 idle samples and 1,939 of 2,022 overrun samples, alternating between 0.90 and 1.10. It only happens below about 64 kPa.
Each time lambda reaches the current target the target flips to the other side, every 5 to 18 s at idle. Lambda sweeps 0.90 to 1.10 as a result.
Idle RPM follows it: about 1,059 rpm at the lean end and 1,166 rpm at the rich end.
findings.why: The ECU is steering the mixture from 10% rich to 10% lean and back. Torque changes with mixture, so idle speed rises and falls with it and the fuel trims never settle.
steps: In the O2 control setup, find the setting that offsets or oscillates the closed-loop target (it may be called target oscillation, dither or switching amplitude). It is acting as ±0.10 λ. Set it to 0 so O2 Control Bank 1 Target equals Target Lambda.
If the oscillation is there for a catalyst, keep it small: a few hundredths of lambda, not 0.10.
Re-log a hot idle. O2 Control Bank 1 Target should read the same as Target Lambda and lambda should hold within about ±0.03.
Do this before changing idle speed or fuel trim gains. Those loops cannot be judged while this swing is driving them.

channels.a: O2 Control Bank 1 Short Term Fuel Trim

findings.title: Idle speed control barely reacts to RPM error
evidence: At a normal, warm-timing idle, RPM sat more than 80 rpm off target for up to 6.5 s at a time.
At about 100 rpm of error the proportional term adds 0.3% output and the integral moves 1.00% per second. Each 1% of output is 0.06% of throttle, so that is 0.02% of throttle.
Over one idle log the integral swings 8.5% to follow a 206 rpm swing, so the engine needs roughly 4.1% of output per 100 rpm.
Idle Control Derivative Gain is 0 and Idle Control Ignition Correction never leaves 0°: idle is held by the throttle alone.
findings.why: A loop this soft lets idle drift 100 rpm or more for seconds at a time. That is what makes an idle feel lazy and lets it sag when a fan or the steering loads the engine.
steps: Fix the closed-loop fuel target swing first. It is the disturbance this loop is chasing, and gains set against it will be wrong once it is gone.

Raise Idle Control Proportional Gain where RPM error is under 120 rpm (logged 40 to 77 there). Aim for about 1.7% of output at 100 rpm of error; it gives 0.3% now, so roughly 4× the gain. Double it, re-log, and repeat rather than jumping straight there.
Raise Idle Control Integral Gain about 2× (logged 90 to 187). At 1.00%/s it takes 4 s to wind in the 4.1% that 100 rpm needs; about 2 s is a good target.
Turn on idle ignition control with about ±5° of authority around the 12° base. Ignition corrects RPM within one engine cycle; the throttle takes several.
Change one thing at a time and re-log a hot idle. Stop raising a gain when a 100 rpm error clears in about a second without RPM overshooting the target.

findings.title: No fuel cut on overrun, running 16% rich
evidence: 1,192 samples with the accelerator released above 1,800 rpm. Injectors stayed on in every one; duty never went below 2.2%.
Lambda averaged 0.84 against a 1.00 target at about 21 kPa.
Decel Detected reads 1 in 1,191 of them, so the ECU recognises the overrun but is not cutting fuel.
findings.why: Fuel injected on overrun does no work. At 16% rich it wastes fuel, can foul plugs, and leaves the wideband reading rich when you get back on the throttle.
steps: Turn on decel fuel cut, or raise its cut amount to 100%. The ECU already flags the decel and reports a Decel Min RPM of 1,300 to 1,750; fuel should be off above that with the accelerator released.

If you keep fuel on during overrun, lean the 20 kPa row of the fuel table instead: 1,500 rpm −9%, 2,000 rpm −17%, 2,500 rpm −20%, 3,000 rpm −17%, 3,500 rpm −13%, 4,000 rpm −17%, 4,500 rpm −11%, 5,000 rpm −11%.
Re-log a lift from about 4,000 rpm. Injector duty should read 0% until RPM falls to the minimum, then come back in without a stumble.

channels.a: Drive By Wire Accelerator Pedal Position

findings.title: 11 fuel table cells are off by 8% or more
evidence: From steady-state samples only, with the O2 trims included. Positive means the cell needs more fuel.
findings.why: When the base table is this far out, the closed-loop trims are doing the fuelling. They react late, so the mixture is wrong every time load changes, and they are not there at all under boost.
steps: Scale each listed cell of the base fuel table by its correction: a −17% cell becomes 0.83 × its current value, a +18% cell 1.18 ×.
80 kPa row: 1,000 rpm +18%.
40 kPa row: 500 rpm −11%.
Drive the same cells again and re-log. Repeat until they are within about ±3%, then let the trims handle the rest.

findings.title: Idle base output is 6% too high at 40 to 50 °C
evidence: Between 40 and 50 °C the base output is 74% and the integral term rests at −6.0% to hold target (282 samples).
Between 50 and 60 °C the base output is 73% and the integral term rests at −8.4% to hold target (1,003 samples).
findings.why: The base table should put the engine at target on its own. When the integral has to carry a standing offset, idle flares or sags each time the controller takes over, until the integral winds back to that offset.
steps: Change Idle Control Base Output at 40 to 50 °C from about 74% to about 68%.
Change Idle Control Base Output at 50 to 60 °C from about 73% to about 65%.
Re-log a warm-up. The integral term should rest within about ±2%.

findings.title: Knock threshold sits within 2 dB of normal engine noise
evidence: Closest: signal 36 dB against a 38 dB threshold at 2,997 rpm, 86 kPa. No knock was counted in any log.
2,500 to 3,000 rpm: background reaches 36 dB, threshold 38 dB near 86 kPa.
3,000 to 3,500 rpm: background reaches 38 dB, threshold 38 dB near 86 kPa.
3,500 to 4,000 rpm: background reaches 40 dB, threshold 40 dB near 94 kPa.
4,000 to 4,500 rpm: background reaches 37 dB, threshold 41 dB near 104 kPa.
4,500 to 5,000 rpm: background reaches 43 dB, threshold 43 dB near 123 kPa.
5,000 to 5,500 rpm: background reaches 43 dB, threshold 45 dB near 153 kPa.
findings.why: A threshold inside normal engine noise makes the ECU pull timing for knock that is not there. Set too far above it, real knock goes unseen. About 6 dB over the background is the usual margin.
steps: Raise the Knock Threshold table to about 6 dB over background in these cells: 2,500 to 3,000 rpm near 86 kPa, from 38 to 43 dB; 3,000 to 3,500 rpm near 86 kPa, from 38 to 44 dB; 3,500 to 4,000 rpm near 94 kPa, from 40 to 47 dB; 4,000 to 4,500 rpm near 104 kPa, from 41 to 43 dB; 4,500 to 5,000 rpm near 123 kPa, from 43 to 49 dB; 5,000 to 5,500 rpm near 153 kPa, from 45 to 49 dB.
Only raise a cell if you are sure the engine was not knocking there. No knock was counted, but under boost check with audio knock detection before trusting the background figure.
Re-log. Knock Sensor 1 Knock Count should stay at 0 in normal driving.

findings.title: Intake cam off target by 10°
evidence: Cam at 29.2° against a 19.0° target at 2,401 rpm, off by more than 5° for 1.0 s.
Around that moment the target moved 11°. The cam itself moves at up to 19°/s in these logs.
With the target steady, error averages −0.5° and varies by ±1.9°.
findings.why: Cam timing sets how much air the engine traps. When the cam is not where the table says, fuel and ignition for that cell are slightly wrong too.
steps: Leave the cam control gains alone (logged P 642, I 40, D 23). With the target steady the cam already holds it.
Smooth the cam target table around 2,500 rpm: neighbouring cells differ by enough that the target jumps 11° as load changes. Keep steps between adjacent cells to about 5°.

checks.title: Torque dip at 3,257 rpm
evidence: Torque fell 13% between 3,066 and 3,257 rpm, then recovered by 3,366 rpm.
Ignition, throttle, MAP and lambda were steady through it, so it may be road surface or gradient.
checks.why: A dip that the engine recovers from is power left on the table, and it usually has one cause you can see in the log.
steps: Repeat the pull on the same road. A dip that moves or disappears is the road; one that stays at the same RPM is the engine.
